terms.gloss: drive home, impress (a point) on someone
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; aliquid alicui (or memoriae alicujus)
evidence: Quint. 6.4.5 (Lewis & Short): firmissima quaeque memoriae jūdicis inculcāre
Cic. de Or. 1.127 (Lewis & Short): id quod trādātur vel etiam inculcētur
terms.comment: To hammer a point in by saying it again and again; Lewis & Short glosses Cic. Att. 16.3.1 “emphasized by additions”. Literally to tread or ram in, and so also to cram in where it doesn’t belong (Graeca verba inculcāre, Cic. Off. 1.111).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with an accusative and infinitive, or the dative of the person pressed
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.32.1 (Lewis & Short): urgē, īnstā, perfice
terms.comment: To keep on at a claim or a task; literally to stand on, then to press hard on an enemy, and of time, to be at hand (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: adverbial phrase, with a verb of asking, saying or thinking
evidence: Cic. Fam. 13.66.2: etiam atque etiam tē rogō atque ōrō ut …
terms.comment: How a Latin speaker underlines a request: said once, it means “I ask you most earnestly”. Latin also stresses a word by putting it first or last, or with ipse and quidem.

phrases.latin: Ego illud sēdulō negāre factum; ille īnstat factum.
phrases.english: I kept denying that it had happened; he insisted it had.

phrases.latin: etiam atque etiam tē rogō atque ōrō ut eum … juvēs
phrases.english: I ask and beg you again and again to help him

sources: Lewis & Short: inculco · Lewis & Short: insto · Lewis & Short: etiam
Ter. And. 146–147 and Cic. Fam. 13.66.2 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026). Neither Morgan–Owens nor Traupman gives a word for “emphasize”.
